Rough around the edges, but the best puzzle game I've played nonetheless.

It's got beautiful aesthetics, intuitive mechanics that feel really satisfying, and some good puzzle design; unfortunately, there's one major thing that makes the game as a whole really unfun to play.

In each world, you have to complete *every* level in order to progress - there's no optional content whatsoever. And the puzzles can be incredibly difficult, so sometimes you'll have to spend hours stuck on a single puzzle, otherwise you can't move on. This sucks. It feels awful when you really want to see what's next but can't because of one stupid puzzle. I'm currently stuck in world 3 with one level left to solve, Cold Frustration. This level is so hard that whenever I open the game now, I end up just spending an hour randomly moving sausages, unable to find a solution. And it's not that I don't like hard puzzles - I've 100%ed Baba Is You for example - it's just that I prefer to save them for later, after progressing through the game first.

In games like Baba Is You and I Wanna Lockpick, worlds have a clear requirement that's less than the total number of levels in the world, so you can choose which levels you complete. If SSR was designed like this, then Cold Frustration would be an optional bonus level, allowing you to skip it. I'd enjoy the game a lot more if that was the case.

As a bonus, here's some very minor things about the game that I also find annoying. This part of the review is not mandatory to read, so you can skip it if you like.
[list]
[*] You can't go back to a level you've already solved in the hub. Luckily, the game automatically makes a backup of your save file every time you solve a level, so you can reload a previous save file to redo a level. It's very cumbersome but it works.
[*] The options menu is very basic. For example, you can't rebind your controls, or turn off the day/night cycle which is distracting sometimes.
[*] The camera angle often obscures important puzzle elements.
[*] For some reason, the game hides your mouse cursor, which makes it difficult to point to things to help organize your thoughts.
[/list]

为什么香肠卷是一个好游戏，他是精美的。整个游戏都围绕着一个核心机制移动香肠徐徐展开。非常符合大众理解，不需要任何附加的说明来理解，学习成本非常的低。然后整个世界谜题都围绕着这一机制铺开。

他不会很生硬的告诉你，[spoiler] 把香肠抵住墙会把叉子插进去 [/spoiler] ，也不会跳出一个菜单跟你说[spoiler] 踩在香肠上能滚动香肠[/spoiler] 。所有的mechanic rules都要你自己去发现，而精妙的关卡设计引导着你去发现。这是一个fair，并且respect player intelligence的游戏。我很喜欢这个游戏no redundancy的设计哲学，可以说地图里的每一个方块，梯子在解谜中都有他独特的用处，想到这一点，玩家和设计者建立了一种非常赤忱的信任，跟随者这些线索我们逐渐瓶凑出解题的思路。这一场与作者深层次的对话，他会奖励每一个留心观察，认真研究彻底游戏机制而不是想着过了就过了的人（我恰恰是这样敲一天钟的和尚，所以游玩前期很痛苦，对我来说也是一次自我成长之旅）。

我觉得如果只是为了爽那大可不必玩香肠，隔壁炸弹毛毛虫等游戏解谜难度不高，有着精妙的关卡设计大幅度降低了负反馈。他们不像香肠卷一样解谜曲线的前期是非常负面的，因为要花很多精力时间去尝试可能的操作然后才是如何把这些操作串联起来解谜，真正解谜的过程其实是在后半段，前面更像是探索与发现。回看已经是十几年的老游戏了，我任然不觉得他过时，甚至依然觉得他处在时代前沿。他极其有深度的内核让我觉得再来十年我任然会满怀热情的打开它在此通关。

Stephen’s Sausage Roll by increpare games is a puzzle game that disguises extraordinary complexity beneath an almost absurdly plain exterior. At first glance, it appears trivial—blocky islands, oversized sausages, and a protagonist wielding what looks like an unwieldy fork. Yet within minutes, it becomes clear that this is not a casual or whimsical experience, but a rigorously designed test of spatial reasoning and logical foresight. It is the kind of game that doesn’t just ask you to solve puzzles—it asks you to fundamentally rethink how you approach them.

The core concept is elegantly simple: sausages must be rolled across grills so that every side is cooked exactly once. That’s the rule, and almost everything in the game flows from it. However, the simplicity of the objective is offset by the intricacy of the movement system. The player character occupies space in a non-traditional way, and every push, pivot, or repositioning of a sausage carries cascading consequences. A single careless move can ruin an entire setup, forcing a restart. The game’s design ensures that every action matters, turning even small decisions into meaningful commitments that must be thought through in advance.

What defines the experience is its uncompromising difficulty. There is no onboarding process, no gradual ramp-up designed to ease players into its logic. Instead, it expects immediate engagement with its rules, leaving players to experiment, fail, and gradually build understanding on their own. This can feel harsh at first, but it also creates a uniquely rewarding learning curve. Each puzzle solved feels like a genuine breakthrough, not because it required quick thinking, but because it demanded sustained effort and careful reasoning. The game doesn’t reward instinct—it rewards patience and clarity of thought.

The level design is where the game truly excels. Every stage feels intentional, constructed to explore a specific idea or variation of the mechanics without unnecessary repetition. New concepts are introduced subtly, often without explanation, allowing players to discover their implications through direct interaction. This approach creates a sense of intellectual progression, where each solved puzzle expands your understanding of what is possible within the system. Despite the limited set of rules, the game manages to maintain a surprising level of variety, constantly challenging players to adapt their thinking rather than rely on established patterns.

Visually, the game is stripped down to the bare essentials. Its low-detail environments and flat color palette might initially seem underwhelming, but this minimalism is entirely deliberate. By removing visual distractions, the game ensures that attention remains fixed on the puzzles themselves. The sparse presentation also contributes to an unusual, almost meditative atmosphere, where the focus shifts entirely to problem-solving. There is a quiet intensity to the experience, as players become absorbed in the logic of each scenario without interruption.

The narrative elements are subtle and enigmatic, existing more as fragments than a fully developed story. Occasional pieces of text appear, hinting at themes that are never fully explained. This ambiguity mirrors the game’s overall design philosophy, which avoids explicit instruction or clear answers. The story, much like the puzzles, invites interpretation rather than providing resolution, adding a layer of intrigue without distracting from the central gameplay.

Despite its many strengths, the game’s demanding nature makes it a difficult recommendation for a broad audience. Its lack of guidance and steep difficulty curve can be discouraging, especially for players who prefer more accessible or immediately gratifying experiences. Progress often requires extended periods of trial and error, and the mental effort involved can be exhausting. However, for those who enjoy deep, methodical challenges, this intensity is precisely what makes the game so compelling.

In the end, Stephen’s Sausage Roll stands as a remarkable example of how far a simple idea can be pushed through thoughtful design. It offers a level of depth and precision that few puzzle games achieve, rewarding persistence with moments of genuine insight and accomplishment. It is not a game that seeks to entertain in a conventional sense, but one that challenges, frustrates, and ultimately satisfies in equal measure.

Over the decade since this game released, hardcore puzzle games like this one have gotten...cursed. An overworld outside the puzzles rather than a simple level select, puzzles interacting with each other, never introducing new mechanics that aren't direct modifications of the main one, never introducing new mechanics at all and sticking to new interactions with the existing ones, "I could've done this the whole time" moments, and so on. You'll find most or all of these in games like Baba Is You, A Monster's Expedition, SquishCraft, Can of Wormholes, I Wanna Lockpick, Maxwell's Puzzling Demon, Gentoo Rescue, and...

...wait what do you mean Stephen's Sausage Roll had all of these already???

This game was truly way ahead of its time. If you got into puzzles since this became widespread, it's what you play them for, and you've written this game off because it supposedly doesn't have this, I urge you to reconsider. I suspect the only reason this game has fallen out of favor is that Baba Is You kind of stole its thunder as The™ hardcore puzzle game. The more recent entries on the list from earlier have very obvious baba inspiration more so than obvious sausage inspiration. However, the earlier ones, including baba itself, were definitely inspired by this game. Personally, I think I preferred that era of puzzle design, as now, baba's approach to metapuzzles has become nearly ubiquitous, whereas before, every game did it slightly differently (I especially applaud Can of Wormholes for how unique its approach is).

But I digress. This game is brutally difficult, I think the only game I've ever played that's topped it is Bean and Nothingness. However, that didn't seem to stop you all with Maxwell's Puzzling Demon (which I haven't yet played, to be fair), so...I'm sure you'll be fine. If you stick with it, you will indeed discover that there's more to this game than meets the eye, and it has the type of twists you'd expect from a more modern puzzle game. One twist in particular, dare I say it, might have even topped Baba Is You's well-known big twist for me. The game truly innovated an absurd amount, and I don't think it deserved to be forgotten about.

Now, unlike all you Icely Puzzles viewers, who seem to [i]only[/i] care about this and nothing else, I do also actually care about the puzzle design itself. In my opinion, this very nearly has the best puzzle design of any game ever. There was one puzzle I found tedious (which is literally the entire reason this game doesn't get a 10/10 from me), but other than that, this game has the highest density of puzzle aha moments of any game I've ever played. Basically every single puzzle felt extremely satisfying to solve. The reasons did vary - the earlier puzzles were so small they almost felt mathematical, and despite that you could actually apply logic to solve them rather than brute forcing them, and the later ones usually focused on new and interesting interactions instead - but again, other than that one, I loved all of them. The only other game that gets anywhere near this degree of utterly brilliant puzzle design is Can of Wormholes, which does actually have zero bad levels imo.

In case it's not clear by now, for the love of god, play this game. It is so underrated nowadays.

Edit 20/4/26: despite this review not showing up on either the store page or the "Most Helpful: Week" section Steam defaults to, and having posted the review a month ago, like 7 different people rated it as helpful just today. Thank you all for that, of course, but where are you finding this? Has it been linked somewhere externally or something? If that is the case I am pretty honored. Comments are open (as they always are on my reviews), so please tell me. (also after playing the game for 40 more hours I did find one more tedious puzzle lol but that's neither here nor there - the rest of the puzzles are still just as amazing)

so you call yourself a puzzle game enjoyer? what's your favorite SSR level then? Wretch's Retreat was a brutal one for me, and stood out the most as a level that felt so seemingly impossible.

If you like puzzle games, you owe it to yourself to play through this one. It's like a more polished more difficult version of A Monster's Expedition, if you've happened to have played that one before SSR like me. 

The first few levels are hard, and force you to become comfortable with the strange control scheme of your character. But this is important, because it is a necessary thing before tackling the future worlds. All levels must be completed to advance, so you just have to grit your teeth through the suffering of the bizarre way the character moves. 

Each world after the first introduces more and more meat to chew on without introducing any "fluff". The last few levels start to feel a little same-y, and the final level is more of a victory lap and a way for you to look back upon the entire experience. The hardest level for me took about 3 hours, with other difficult levels typically taking at most an hour each. My patience has been rewarded.

Truly a puzzle masterpiece.

Stephen's Sausage Roll é exatamente o que sua descrição sugere: um simples jogo de puzzle 3D - mas apesar de sua simplicidade mecânica, o jogo consegue criar uma das experiências de quebra-cabeça mais difíceis e recompensadoras que eu já joguei em toda a minha vida.

Suas habilidades permanecem as mesmas até o final do jogo, com o jogador podendo se mexer nas quatro direções e girar seu garfo, mas a magia está nas coisas que você vai descobrindo que sempre conseguiu fazer com estas ações e nunca soube. A mecânica principal aqui é usada e explorada de todas as formas possíveis, e chega a ser inspirador ver o quão longe ela é levada até o final - com esses elementos sendo ensinados ao jogador por meio do level design perfeito e extremamente bem planejado do jogo.

Os gráficos do jogo podem não ser tão agradáveis, e seu preço é bem caro (esperem uma promoção), mas para quem quer uma das melhores e mais difíceis experiências que vai ter jogando um jogo de puzzle, eu recomendo muito Stephen's Sausage Roll. Apesar de sua dificuldade eu recomendo evitar procurar as respostas, não existem achievements aqui então a única recompensa que o jogador vai ter é a satisfação de finalmente entender a solução de uma fase e completar ela do seu próprio jeito.

Truly one of the greatest puzzle games. It's got a bit of a slow start, where it leans a bit too much into being a standard and slightly frustrating block-pusher, and some early puzzles can feel a bit trial-and-error. But as it evolves, it shows so much more depth. A relatively simple set of mechanics interact to allow so much intricate innovation. Every puzzle reveals something for you to understand about the game and how it works. And it keeps escalating that discovery past where you'd expect it to stop, you think you've been shown everything but there's more. 

It is such a well-crafted experience. It's hard but rarely feels unfair, as puzzles don't have lots of fluff and instead have so few moving parts that it often feels baffling that you can't figure out the right path.
